The allocation model of [Where do residents register?](allocation-workflow.html)
uses a Gaussian decay and small areas. This guide shows how to change both.
You will declare a decay kernel of your own and fit it, fit the model on a
population grid instead of small areas, and map a fitted model's outputs on
that grid. The last section says where demand groups fit in. The guide uses
the registrations, travel times and grids of [The Cornwall GP example
data](cornwall-data.html). The `spax()` interface and the allocation model are
experimental and may change in later versions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The model to extend

The starting point is the conditional logit model (CLM) fitted to the
registrations of mainland Cornwall. Demand is the number of residents of each
small area registered with a GP practice, and supply is each practice's GP
full-time equivalents (FTE), excluding GPs in training. Each practice attracts
residents in proportion to its supply times a decay weight of the travel time,
and an outside option, registration with a practice outside mainland
Cornwall, takes the rest with a weight v0 of its own. The inputs are those of
the other allocation guides.

```{r inputs}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
```

The default specification has a Gaussian decay whose travel scale σ, in
minutes, sets how fast the weight falls with travel time. σ is fitted together
with the outside weight v0.

```{r gaussian}
# Gaussian decay and outside weight, both fitted to the registrations
clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
coef(clm)
```

The message about the Isles of Scilly is explained in [Where do residents
register?](allocation-workflow.html#fit-the-model); the later fits on the same
data print it too.

The fitted σ is `r round(coef(clm)[["sigma"]], 1)` minutes. The next section
fits a kernel of your own to the same data and compares the two fits.

## Your own decay

A decay kernel turns a travel time into a weight. spax has built-in
Gaussian, exponential and power kernels, whose σ can be fitted.
`decay_kernel()` declares your own
from an R function of `distance` and `sigma`, and `decay_custom()` puts it in
a model specification. The kernel below gives full weight to every practice
within 3 minutes, where a minute more or less hardly matters, and falls as a
Gaussian curve beyond that, with σ the scale of the fall.

```{r plateau-declare}
# Full weight within `plateau` minutes, Gaussian decay beyond
plateau_weight <- function(distance, sigma, plateau) {
  ifelse(
    distance <= plateau,
    1,
    exp(-(distance - plateau)^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
  )
}

plateau_kernel <- decay_kernel(
  plateau_weight,
  name = "plateau",
  parameter = "scale",
  args = list(plateau = 3)
)
plateau_kernel
```

The print shows what the declaration stores: the function's code as text,
which is rebuilt into a function whenever the kernel is used. So the function
can use only its arguments, base R, `pkg::fn` calls and the fixed values in
`args`, not objects from your workspace. A result that uses the kernel carries
this code and runs it when used again, so read saved results only from
sources you trust. `?decay_kernel` lists the other rules.

`decay_custom()` takes the place of `decay_gaussian()` in `spec_clm()`, and
σ and v0 are fitted as before.

```{r plateau-fit, message = FALSE}
# The plateau kernel in place of the Gaussian, with sigma and v0 fitted
clm_plateau <- spax(d, spec_clm(decay = decay_custom(plateau_kernel)),
  observed = flows)
clm_plateau
```

```{r plateau-values, include = FALSE}
sigma_gaussian <- coef(clm)[["sigma"]]
sigma_plateau <- coef(clm_plateau)[["sigma"]]
gaussian_at_9 <- exp(-9^2 / (2 * sigma_gaussian^2))
plateau_at_9 <- plateau_weight(9, sigma_plateau, plateau = 3)
```

The plateau kernel's σ is `r round(sigma_plateau, 2)` minutes, against
`r round(sigma_gaussian, 2)` for the Gaussian kernel. Each σ sets the scale of
its own kernel's fall. The plateau kernel starts falling only at 3 minutes, so
a smaller σ does not mean less weight at a given time.

The plot shows the two fitted kernels.

```{r kernels, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Line chart of decay weight against travel time from 0 to 20 minutes for the two fitted kernels. The Gaussian kernel falls smoothly from 1; the plateau kernel stays at 1 up to 3 minutes and then falls, lying above the Gaussian curve until both are close to 0 at about 15 minutes."}
# Each fitted kernel's weight from 0 to 20 minutes
minutes <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.1)
curves <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    minutes,
    kernel = "Gaussian",
    weight = exp(-minutes^2 / (2 * sigma_gaussian^2))
  ),
  data.frame(
    minutes,
    kernel = "Plateau",
    weight = plateau_weight(minutes, sigma_plateau, plateau = 3)
  )
)

ggplot(curves, aes(minutes, weight, color = kernel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x = "Travel time (minutes)",
    y = "Decay weight",
    color = "Fitted kernel"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

At 9 minutes the plateau kernel keeps `r sprintf("%.2f", plateau_at_9)` of
its weight, the Gaussian kernel `r sprintf("%.2f", gaussian_at_9)`.

`compare_fits()` sets fits side by side. Given results of `spax()`, it takes
each model from its result and checks that both fits use the same
registrations, loss and travel times. The loss measures how far the fitted
registrations are from the observed ones. Lower is closer, and the table gives
each fit's loss difference from the first fit.

```{r plateau-compare}
# Loss differences are measured from the first fit, the Gaussian
comparison <- compare_fits(list(gaussian = clm, plateau = clm_plateau))
as.data.frame(comparison)[
  c("specification", "parameters", "loss_difference", "count_correlation")
]
```

```{r compare-values, include = FALSE}
compared <- as.data.frame(comparison)
```

The plateau fit's loss is higher by
`r format(round(compared$loss_difference[2]), big.mark = ",")`, and its
fitted registrations by area and practice correlate with the observed ones at
`r sprintf("%.2f", compared$count_correlation[2])`, against
`r sprintf("%.2f", compared$count_correlation[1])` for the Gaussian fit. On
these data the Gaussian kernel fits better. [Reading
results](reading-results.html#what-a-fit-shows-and-what-it-does-not) says
what such a comparison can show.

## Fitting on raster data

An allocation model can also run on a population grid. `prep_data()` takes a
population raster and a travel stack, a raster with one layer of travel
minutes per practice. Each populated cell becomes an origin, a place residents
start from, so no small areas are needed. The chunk is the grid recipe of the
other guides, copied whole.

```{r grid-inputs}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
```

The recipe ends with `grid_data`, the input of the floating catchment area
(FCA) indices, whose demand is WorldPop's estimate of residents in 2020. A fit
needs demand that counts the same people as the observations, so the next
chunk prepares the same grid again with its demand rescaled.

The observations here are practice totals: the mainland residents registered
at each mainland practice, summed from `cornwall_flows`. The list sizes in
`cornwall_gp` would also count patients who live outside mainland Cornwall.
The grid is scaled to the sum of the totals, so the grid says where these
residents live and the totals say how many there are.

```{r grid-data}
# Registrations of mainland residents at each mainland practice
practice_totals <- cornwall_flows |>
  filter(lsoa %in% areas$lsoa, practice %in% gp$practice) |>
  group_by(practice) |>
  summarise(patients = sum(patients))
totals <- obs_totals(practice_totals, facility = "practice", count = "patients")
totals

# The grid scaled to the same residents: where they live, not how many
grid_residents <- global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
registered_grid <- pop * sum(practice_totals$patients) / grid_residents
registered_data <- prep_data(registered_grid, gp, travel_grid,
  id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
registered_data
```

The prepared data hold the rasters as they are. `spax()` turns the cells with
residents into origins each time it runs a model on them.

The grid was scaled so that every resident counted is registered at a
mainland practice. That leaves nothing for an outside option, so this section
fits the Huff model, which has none. It shares each cell's residents among the
practices in proportion to attraction times decay weight. By default
`spec_huff()` fits a power decay, whose σ is an exponent (the weight is the
travel time to the
power −σ), and an attractiveness exponent β (the attraction is GP FTE to the
power β).

```{r grid-fit}
# Huff model on the grid, fitted to the practice totals
huff_grid <- spax(registered_data, spec_huff(), observed = totals)
huff_grid
```

```{r grid-values, include = FALSE}
huff_sigma <- coef(huff_grid)[["sigma"]]
huff_beta <- coef(huff_grid)[["beta"]]
n_cells <- nrow(as.data.frame(huff_grid, type = "origins"))
huff_starts <- as.data.frame(huff_grid, type = "starts")
```

The `r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` populated cells are the origins,
named by their cell numbers. Of the `r nrow(huff_starts)` starting points,
`r sum(huff_starts$eligible)` converged, and `spax()` keeps the best of them.
`as.data.frame(huff_grid, type = "starts")` lists all
`r nrow(huff_starts)`.

A σ of `r round(huff_sigma, 2)` means that a
practice twice as far away gets `r round(2^-huff_sigma, 2)` of the weight. A
β of `r round(huff_beta, 2)` means that a practice with twice the GP FTE
attracts `r round(2^huff_beta, 2)` times as many residents, other things
equal.

Totals say how many residents each practice has, not where they live.
`check_fit()` asks whether travel time matters to the fit. It compares the
fit, on the same loss, with an allocation without distance decay and with one
in proportion to attraction alone.

```{r grid-check}
huff_check <- check_fit(huff_grid)
huff_check
```

```{r grid-check-values, include = FALSE}
grid_check <- as.data.frame(huff_check)
```

Every cell reaches every practice, so the two simpler allocations coincide
here and their rows match. Both reproduce the totals less well: their loss is
higher by `r format(round(min(grid_check$loss_difference[-1])), big.mark = ",")`,
so travel time matters to this fit, and their median trip is
`r grid_check$trip_median[2]` minutes against the fit's
`r grid_check$trip_median[1]`. The `contact` column, the share of residents
modeled to use a practice in the data, is 1 because the Huff model has no
outside option.

The travel of the origins is held as a matrix of
`r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells by `r nrow(gp)` practices, about
`r round(n_cells * nrow(gp) * 8 / 1e6, 1)` MB, and a fit needs about 8 times
its memory or more (see `?prep_data`). Crop or coarsen a much larger grid
first. [Grid resolution and computational cost](grid-resolution.html) shows
what a coarser grid changes.

## Maps on the grid

A fitted model predicts at any place that has travel times to its practices.
Every populated cell of the grid has them, so the small-area fit `clm` can map
its outside share across the grid. `predict()` takes a travel matrix with one
row per cell. `spatial` says which raster cell each row is, and
`type = "raster"` returns a map on the grid.

```{r grid-predict, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Raster map of mainland Cornwall on the grid of about 1 km cells, colored by the outside share that the small-area fit predicts at each populated cell, in percent; most cells are below 1%, and the share rises above 20% in cells far from every practice: around Bodmin Moor and inland in the north-east, at the western tip and on the north coast around Padstow."}
# Travel from each populated cell to each practice, rows named by cell number
populated <- which(values(pop)[, 1] > 0)
grid_travel <- values(travel_grid)[populated, ]
rownames(grid_travel) <- populated

# The small-area fit's outside share at every populated cell, as a raster
grid_outside <- predict(clm, grid_travel,
  outputs = "outside_share",
  spatial = list(template = pop, cell_index = populated),
  type = "raster"
)

# Mainland Cornwall's outline, in the grid's longitude and latitude
outline <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_transform(crs(pop)) |>
  vect()
plot(
  100 * grid_outside,
  breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100),
  col = hcl.colors(7, "Mako", rev = TRUE),
  axes = FALSE,
  main = "Modeled outside share, grid of about 1 km",
  plg = list(title = "Outside\nshare (%)")
)
lines(outline, lwd = 0.6)
```

```{r grid-predict-values, include = FALSE}
share_below_1 <- mean(values(grid_outside, mat = FALSE)[populated] < 0.01)
area_share_max <- max(as.data.frame(clm, type = "origins")$outside_share)
```

In `r round(100 * share_below_1)`% of the cells the modeled outside
share is below 1%. It rises only far from every practice: around Bodmin Moor
and inland in the north-east, at the western tip and on the north coast around
Padstow.

The table counts the cells where more than half of the residents are modeled
to register outside mainland Cornwall, and their share of the grid's
residents.

```{r grid-share}
# Cells with an outside share above one half, and their share of residents
cell_share <- values(grid_outside, mat = FALSE)[populated]
cell_residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)[populated]
far_out <- cell_share > 0.5
data.frame(
  cells = sum(far_out),
  residents_percent = round(100 * sum(cell_residents[far_out]) / sum(cell_residents), 2)
)
```

The `r sum(far_out)` cells above one half hold
`r round(100 * sum(cell_residents[far_out]) / sum(cell_residents), 2)`% of the
grid's residents. Their share is high because the fitted travel scale is short
and the outside weight is the same everywhere. No small area is modeled above
`r round(100 * area_share_max)`%, so these values extend the model to places
unlike the areas it was fitted to: read them as extrapolation.

## Demand groups

Residents can differ in how far they travel, for example by age. The
allocation model takes demand groups in three places:

- `prep_data()`: demand as a named list of vectors, one per group, and travel
  as one matrix for all groups or a named list of them.
- `spec_clm()`: a named list of decays, one per group, or `by_group = "sigma"`
  (or `"v0"`) to let one fitted parameter differ by group.
- `observed`: counts by group, from `obs_totals()` with a group column or a
  matrix of facilities by groups.

A parameter that differs by group can be fitted only to counts recorded by
group. The small areas have ONS population estimates by age band (`pop_0_15`,
`pop_16_64` and `pop_65p` in `cornwall_lsoa`), but the registrations are not
split by age, so this guide fits no groups. The FCA indices take demand groups
on the grid, and [Which FCA index?](fca-methods.html#several-demand-groups)
shows them.
